result: In a large female cohort, CFS patients reached roughly half the maximal workload and peak VO2 of matched sedentary controls, with higher resting but lower maximal heart rate; the result held in those meeting maximal-effort criteria (RQ>=1.0, >=85% predicted HR).
reason: Independent case-control cohort, same measure (peak VO2 and low peak HR), same direction; not among cited studies.

result: In 32 CFS vs 32 controls on capnography head-up tilt, supine values were similar, but on tilt patients had significantly lower systolic and diastolic BP and end-tidal CO2 and larger rises in HR and respiratory rate.
reason: Independent cohort shows the same tilt-induced end-tidal CO2 fall; no CBF data, so it supports only the hypocapnia part of the claim.

result: In 32 CFS vs 32 controls on capnography head-up tilt, patients developed lower BP and end-tidal CO2 and higher HR and respiratory rate on tilt.
reason: already cited (Naschitz 2000 is named in the finding detail as a tilt ETCO2 study)

result: 66 non-psychiatric CFS patients had reduced exercise capacity and greater perceived effort than 30 sedentary controls but were 'equally unfit' (similar aerobic fitness), and low capacity was linked to quadriceps weakness, cardiovascular response and BMI.
reason: Peak aerobic fitness did not differ from sedentary controls, which is a null result on the finding's measure, not an extension.

result: CFS patients were weaker than sedentary and depressed controls and as unfit as sedentary controls; the authors conclude deconditioning helps maintain disability, with GET-related gains tied to lower submaximal heart rate.
reason: Paper argues for a deconditioning explanation, which runs against the finding's claim that deconditioning alone does not explain the abnormalities.

result: In 14 adolescents with CFS and 22 with POTS vs 30 controls, R-R interval and HRV were reduced supine and on tilt, LF BP variability was raised and vagal baroreflex transfer was attenuated, with HRV lowest in CFS.
reason: Same direction for reduced HRV, but in an adolescent subgroup and adds a baroreflex mechanism, so extends rather than replicates.

result: In 73 CFS vs 21 controls, the GH response to insulin hypoglycaemia (peak 17.0 vs 22.1 ug/l, p=0.01; AUC p=0.002) and nocturnal GH AUC (p=0.045) were lower, while arginine and clonidine responses and IGF-I were normal; prolactin and TSH were higher.
reason: Same GH-stimulation measure, same direction as Allain 1997, with IGF-I normal as in Cleare; larger patient group than Cleare 2000, so the claim about the 'largest controlled study' may need revisiting. Not Moorkens 1998.

result: Resting SPECT in 30 non-depressed CFS, 12 depressed and 15 controls showed increased perfusion in the right thalamus, pallidum and putamen and left thalamus in CFS, not reduced perfusion.
reason: Same measure (resting SPECT CBF) with the opposite direction (increased regional perfusion).

result: In a blinded study, a 37 kDa 2-5A-binding protein was present in PBMC extracts of 88% (50/57) of CFS patients vs 28% (15/53) of controls, 11% of healthy subjects and none with depression or fibromyalgia.
reason: Independent cohort detects the low-molecular-weight RNase L-related protein in CFS PBMC, same direction as the cited 1990s work.

result: Two-night PSG plus MSLT in 46 unselected CFS outpatients found AHI>=5 in 46%, periodic limb movements in 5% and MSLT<10 min in 30%, but neither primary sleep disorders nor sleepiness were associated with fatigue, mood or function scales.
reason: Uncontrolled PSG series that adds evidence that the sleep disorders found do not explain CFS symptoms, which fits the finding's second sentence.
